episodes.167449: During the morning of Monday, May 9th, a small complex of thunderstorms that developed across eastern South Dakota moved eastward and affected a large area of west-central, central and east-central Minnesota before moving into west-central Wisconsin late Monday morning. Although scattered thunderstorms developed south and north of this main supercell storm, this storm in particular was the main producing of large hail, up to baseball size, that fell from shortly after sunrise in far west-central Minnesota, to east-central Minnesota, north of the Twin Cities, by 10 AM. This storm continued to pulse up and down from tops as high as 60,000 feet. Damage was widespread where the large hailstone fell.
episodes.167450: The main severe storm that moved across portions of southern and central Minnesota, then moved across west-central Wisconsin and produced large hail, up to ping pong size, before weakening in northern Wisconsin. Strong winds damaged a number of farms.  There was a brief tornado north of Saint Croix Falls, which damaged three farms.
episodes.167451: A dry-line/cold front was moving across Minnesota during the afternoon of Monday, May 9th. A few thunderstorms developed along this front across central Minnesota, and quickly spread south and eastward during the late afternoon and evening over eastern Minnesota, and adjacent west central Wisconsin. A brief funnel cloud was observed south of Gilman, and a tornado impacted Dakota County between Hastings and Miesville. Large hail and a few damaging wind gusts occurred along this line as it moved eastward. The largest hail stone was 2 inches in diameter and occurred near St. Paul downtown airport.
episodes.167452: A dry-line/cold front that spawn a couple of tornadoes in eastern Minnesota, moved across west central Wisconsin during the evening and produced an additional three tornadoes, plus wind damage, and large hail. The tornadoes occurred near Lake Pepin, near Knapp, and between Colfax and Elk Mound in Dunn County.
episodes.167525: Strong thunderstorms moved across the Nebraska Panhandle on the evening of the 8th with a storm becoming severe across Box Butte County after 10 PM MDT producing ping pong ball sized hail and strong winds in excess of 80 mph from Alliance to Hemingford.
episodes.167619: A slow moving low pressure system, along with plenty of moisture, allowed for showers and thunderstorms to gradually move through the Ohio Valley during the day on May 6th. Heavy rainfall occurred with these storms and additional storm and shower activity developed over the same areas. A swath of 3 to 4 inches of rain fell in a narrow corridor from Huntington northeastward to Elkins, with a few isolated pockets of 4 to 5 reported. This led to considerable flash flooding. A few stronger storms also developed, one of which led to an area of tree damage in Randolph County.||Multiple water rescues took place throughout the Metro Valley, including a man who was swept away while working on his tractor in Cabell County. Additionally, several vehicles were submerged in flood waters and over one hundred homes were impacted by high water with the hardest hit area being the Enslow Park community of Huntington. Flooding occurred across many roadways throughout West Virginia, leaving multiple roads impassable for a time until the water receded.||Even after the rain had concluded, several rivers in the state rose out of their banks for the next several days. This resulted in flooding along areas adjacent to the rivers.
episodes.167756: An unseasonal cold upper-level trough and associated front moved through Northwest California. The system brought lower snow levels and post-frontal hail showers. Small hail covered roadways caused a couple of accidents.
episodes.167905: A dust devil directly impacted a Texas Tech University West Texas mesonet site near Wolfforth. The mesonet site measured a one minute wind gust of 58 mph at 1100 CST.
episodes.168266: Hail, up to the size of golf balls in Garden City, was associated with a series of supercell storms that formed during the early morning hours of May 9th. Storms also produced winds up to 62 mph. The overall system also helped generate some post-frontal non-thunderstorm wind gusts up to 67 mph near Sisseton and 62 mph in Turnerville later that afternoon.
episodes.168565: Isolated thunderstorms developed during the late afternoon hours of May 7th over the northern Nebraska Panhandle. Storms developed in advance of an approaching cold front which lifted across western and central Nebraska during the nighttime hours. As storms tracked east of the panhandle, they organized into a line of strong to severe thunderstorms which stretched from north central Nebraska into southwestern Nebraska. Hail up to golf ball size and wind gusts to around 70 MPH were reported.
episodes.168627: Thunderstorms developed over the northern Nebraska Panhandle and tracked across far northern Nebraska during the early morning hours of May 9th. Golf ball size hail and wind gusts to around 70 MPH were reported with the strongest storms.
episodes.168667: Showers and thunderstorms developed in an area of convergence near the far upper Florida Keys as outflow from showers and thunderstorms over mainland south Florida moved southward. A waterspout developed and was observed making landfall along the oceanside of a community within Key Largo.
episodes.168808: A short-wave trough moved through southwest flow aloft leading to thunderstorm development over the James River Valley. One storm became a low-top supercell thunderstorm, which produced one-inch diameter hail over Stutsman County.
episodes.169010: A low pressure system moving out of the Central Plains brought a warm front through northern Minnesota during the morning hours of the 9th. Supported by a strong low level jet and warm air pushing into the region, storms spread north through the morning hours. Storms produced hail as large as gold balls and damaging winds before losing strength during the late morning as they moved into the Arrowhead.
episodes.169011: A low pressure system moving out of the Central Plains brought a warm front through Minnesota and northwest Wisconsin during the morning hours. Supported by a strong low level jet and warm air pushing into the region, storms spread north through the morning hours. The first round of storms mainly produced hail with the largest being tennis ball sized. A cold front associated with the low then moved through during the afternoon leading to another round of storms that produced hail to the size of quarters. Insurance companies estimated $10 million in property and automobile claims from the storms in Washburn County alone.
episodes.169282: Thunderstorms developing along a frontal boundary turned severe, forming large hail over portions of central Upper Michigan during the late afternoon and evening of the 10th.
episodes.169618: Routed water from heavier early-spring precipitation well to the north brought sections of the James River above flood stage for the first time in nearly two years.
episodes.169941: Scattered thunderstorms developed in south central South Dakota the last half of the night, and moved northeast along the nose of a strong low-level jet toward east central South Dakota and southwest Minnesota after sunrise.  Elevated instability of 1000-2000J/kg and deep-layer elevated shear of 30-40 knots led to organization of storms into multicell structures capable of spotty large hail and damaging wind.

episodes.170207: A strong upper low, and the associated negatively tilted trough, led to the development of severe thunderstorms during the afternoon and evening of May 8. These storms persisted into the morning of May 9, producing severe wind, hail and tornadoes.

events.narrative: The Ohio River at Point Pleasant rose above its 40 foot flood stage on the evening of May 8th. The river would remain out of its banks until the early morning hours of May 10th and crested at 41.7 feet. This resulted in minor flooding around low lying spots of Point Pleasant, including the town's amphitheater.

A thin, rope tornado was seen while looking to the north by northwest, from the intersection of 44th st SE and 106th ave SE. Touchdown was brief and lasted less than one minute. Movement was to the northeast. Public photos and videos documented the brief touchdown near Kee Lake, 4 miles south of I-29. Maximum width was 10 yards, with winds up to 65 mph.

As water from early spring rains and late winter snowmelt in North Dakota and far northern South Dakota routed downstream, the James River at Huron (gage site HURS2) climbed into minor flood stage on May 9, and reached 1.85 feet above flood stage at the end of the month. Significant amounts of agricultural land were inundated. Minor flooding continued at the end of the month.

A non-supercell-spawned waterspout was observed to have made landfall on the Atlantic side of Key Largo in the Silver Shores Community.  A spray ring was visible with the waterspout prior to landfall.  Photos revealed damage to a dock railing and a snapped mature coconut palm tree, but no damage to nearby homes was observed.  Based on all available information, the tornado was rated EF-0 with maximum winds of 60 to 70 mph.
